S067.name: Preoccupation_with_Appearance
S067.description: Preoccupation with one or more perceived defects or flaws in physical appearance that are not observable or appear slight to others.

subtypes.Skin Defects: Excessive preoccupation with practically invisible acne, scars, or complexion.
subtypes.Facial Features: Preoccupation with the shape or size of the nose, eyes, or mouth, which appear normal to others.
subtypes.Asymmetry: Excessive obsession with the face or body not being perfectly symmetrical.
subtypes.Muscle Dysmorphia: The belief that one's body is too small or insufficiently muscular despite being normal or muscular.
subtypes.Specific Body Parts: Obsession that specific parts like hair, teeth, or chest are ugly or abnormal.

S068.name: Appearance_Related_Repetitive_Behaviors
S068.description: Repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed in response to appearance concerns.

subtypes.Mirror Checking or Avoidance: Compulsively checking oneself in the mirror frequently or, conversely, avoiding mirrors strictly.
subtypes.Excessive Camouflaging: Spending excessive time and effort to hide perceived flaws using makeup, clothes, hats, or sunglasses.
subtypes.Skin Picking: Picking or manipulating the skin excessively to remove or 'fix' flaws.
subtypes.Reassurance Seeking: Repetitively asking others for confirmation that one's appearance is okay or not strange.
subtypes.Comparing: Constantly comparing one's body parts with those of passersby or celebrities.
subtypes.Seeking Cosmetic Procedures: Repeatedly seeking or receiving plastic surgery or dermatological procedures.

symptom.disease_info: Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD) is characterized by a persistent, excessive preoccupation with perceived defects in physical appearance that are minimal or not observable to others, leading to marked distress or impairment. Individuals commonly engage in repetitive behaviors (such as mirror checking, grooming, skin picking, or seeking reassurance) or mental acts (such as comparing themselves to others) in response to these concerns. Onset is often in adolescence or early adulthood, with a typically chronic course that can wax and wane in intensity and is frequently exacerbated by social evaluation, transitions, or appearance-focused environments. BDD is distinguished from normal appearance concerns and eating disorders by the disproportionate distress, time consumption, and functional impairment related to specific perceived flaws, and from psychotic disorders by generally intact reality testing outside of appearance beliefs, though insight can range from good to delusional.

patient.stressor: Eric traces the intensification of his appearance concerns to the period surrounding his divorce three years ago, when his ex-wife began dating a younger, very fit partner and friends made casual jokes about him "going gray overnight." As a middle-aged advisor working with affluent clients and mingling at gallery openings, he became acutely aware of being photographed for firm marketing materials and social events, interpreting any glance or pause as a silent judgment about how he looked compared with his clients and peers. Over time, he started turning down speaking engagements, avoiding social gatherings where photos might be taken, and scheduling client meetings only by phone, which began to hurt his book of business and drew criticism from his firm’s partners. When his teenage daughter asked why he never wanted to be in family pictures anymore and his supervisor warned him that his withdrawal was jeopardizing his position, he finally sought psychiatric help, describing that his life had become dominated by worry about a specific aspect of his appearance.
patient.chief_complaint: “I spend so much time checking and trying to fix this one thing about how I look that it’s taking over my day and costing me work.”

S067.name: Preoccupation_with_Appearance
S067.description: Preoccupation with one or more perceived defects or flaws in physical appearance that are not observable or appear slight to others.
S067.manifestation: It feels like the first thing anyone notices about me is how old and worn-out my face looks now—especially the deep lines and the gray at my temples—and even though people tell me they barely see it, I’m constantly imagining them comparing me to my ex’s new, younger boyfriend or my polished, good-looking clients and thinking I look like I’ve let myself go.

S068.name: Appearance_Related_Repetitive_Behaviors
S068.description: Repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed in response to appearance concerns.
S068.manifestation: Most days I lose hours standing in the bathroom mirror, taking selfies under different lighting, trying different hair products or angles to hide the gray and the lines, changing shirts over and over, and then texting my daughter or a coworker for the tenth time, asking if I look too old for the headshots or client meeting, until I’m so frustrated and late that I cancel the event altogether.
